Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verse 1–4:

(p-113) Surat al-Zumar

Makkiyyah according to al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAta' and Jabir. Ibn ʿAbbas said: except for two verses which were revealed in Madinah, one of them being ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement﴾, and the other ﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ to the end of the verse. Others said: except for seven verses from His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ to the end of the seven.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾. The Book is the Qur'an, and it was so named because it is written (maktub).

﴿from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

One: Mighty in His dominion, Wise in His command.

The second: Mighty in His retribution, Wise in His justice.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So worship Allah, making your religion sincerely His﴾. In this there are two interpretations: (p-114) One: It is sincerity in monotheism (tawhid), said by al-Suddi.

The second: sincerity of intention for His sake. And in His saying ﴿His religion﴾ there are two interpretations:

One: His is the obedience, said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: the worship.

﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the pure religion﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

One: the testimony that there is no god but Allah, said by Qatadah.

The second: Islam, said by al-Hasan.

The third: the acts of obedience that are free of showing off (riya').

﴿And those who take protectors other than Him﴾ meaning: deities that they worship.

﴿We do not worship them except that they bring us nearer to Allah in closeness﴾. The disbelievers of Quraysh said this about their idols, and those before them said it about those they worshipped among the angels, ʿUzayr and ʿIsa, meaning: our worship of them is so that they bring us near to Allah in closeness. In this there are three interpretations:

One: that "zulfa" (closeness) here means intercession, said by Qatadah.

The second: that it means rank (manzilah), said by al-Suddi.

The third: that it means nearness (qurb), said by Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verses 5–6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾, has three interpretations:

First: He makes the night carry over the day and the day carry over the night. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

(p-115) Second: The night covers the day, removing its light, and the day covers the night, removing its darkness. This is the view of Qatadah.

Third: It is the decrease of one of them relative to the other, so that the decrease of the night becomes an increase in the day, and the decrease of the day becomes an increase in the night. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: He gathers the night until the day spreads out, and gathers the day until the night spreads out.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created you from a single soul﴾, means from Adam.

﴿Then He made from it its mate﴾, means Hawwa (Eve).

Regarding this there are two views:

First: that He created her from the rib of the back of Adam, which is the lowest of the ribs. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Second: that He created her from the same substance from which Adam was created, so the meaning of His saying ﴿made from it﴾ is "from its like." This is the view of Ibn Bahr.

﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾. Qatadah said: two of the camels, two of the cattle, two of the sheep, and two of the goats, each one being a pair.

Regarding His saying ﴿sent down﴾ there are two views:

First: it means "made." This is the view of al-Hasan.

Second: that He sent them down after creating them in Paradise. This is reported by Ibn ʿIsa.

﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

First: a drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then bones, then flesh. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Suddi.

Second: creation in the wombs of your mothers after your creation in the loins of Adam. This is the view of al-Suddi.

It may also bear a third meaning: creation in the loins of the father, then creation in the womb of the mother, then creation after birth.

﴿In three darknesses﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

First: the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid and Qatadah.

Second: the darkness of the man's loins, the darkness of the woman's belly, and the darkness of the womb. This is reported by Ibn ʿIsa.

It may also bear a third meaning: that they are the darkness of the night's gloom which surrounds the darkness of the placenta, the darkness of the inner organs, and the darkness of the belly.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verses 7–8:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance﴾. On it there are three interpretations:

First: "turning to Him sincerely." This was said by al-Dahhak.

Second: "seeking help from Him." This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: "turning toward Him." This was said by al-Kalbi and Qutrub.

﴿Then when He bestows upon him a blessing from Himself, he forgets what he used to call upon Him for before﴾. On it there are two interpretations:

One: "When a blessing reaches him, he abandons supplication." This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: "When well-being reaches him, he forgets the harm." (Note: the commentary repeats the al-Kalbi attribution at this point.)

Al-Takhwil (تَخْوِيل) is a great gift, whether a grant or a bestowal. Abu al-Najm said:

He gave and did not withhold, and did not withhold, a heap of summits of the bestowed gifts of the one who bestows.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verse 9:

One of them: it is the alif of interrogation (istifham).

The second: it is the alif of address (nida').

(p-117) Regarding qanit (devoutly obedient), there are four views:

The first: it means obedient (al-muti'), as said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: it means humble and submissive (khashi') in his prayer, as said by Ibn Shihab.

The third: it means standing in his prayer, as said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

The fourth: it means one who supplicates to his Lord (al-da'i li-rabbihi).

﴿Through the hours of the night﴾ (ana'a al-layl): there are three views concerning it:

The first: the edges of the night (tarf al-layl), as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the hours of the night (sa'at al-layl), as said by al-Hasan.

The third: what lies between Maghrib and 'Isha', as said by Mansur.

﴿Prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾. al-Suddi said: he fears the punishment of the Hereafter and hopes for the bliss of Paradise.

Concerning the one whom this speech is intended, there are five sayings:

The first: that he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), related by Yahya ibn Sallam.

The second: Abu Bakr, said by Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of al-Dahhak from him.

The third: 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, said by Ibn 'Umar.

The fourth: 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Suhayb, Abu Dharr and Ibn Mas'ud, said by al-Kalbi.

The fifth: that it is general (mursal) concerning whoever is in this state, devoutly standing through the hours of the night.

As for whoever holds that the first alif is an interrogative, he has supposed in the speech an elided response (jawab mahdhuf), its estimate being: "Is one who is devoutly standing through the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, like one who sets up rivals to Allah?" This is said by Yahya.

Ibn 'Isa said: the elided part of the response is: "like one who is not so."

As for whoever holds that the alif is for address, he does not posit an elided response, and he makes the estimate of the speech: "Is one who is devoutly standing through the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord?"

﴿Say: Are those who know and those who do not know equal?﴾ Concerning it there are three views:

The first: "Are those who know this and act upon it equal to those who do not know this and therefore do not act upon it?" as said by Qatadah.

The second: that those who know are the believers, who know that they will meet their Lord, and those who do not (p-118) know are the polytheists who set up rivals to Allah, said by Yahya.

The third: what Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali said: "Those who know are us, and those who do not know are our enemies."

And it may bear a fourth: that those who know are those who are certain (al-muqinun), and those who do not know are the doubters (al-murtabun).

The Lord, Exalted and Majestic, says: ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: its meaning is, for those who do good in this world there is good in the Hereafter, which is Paradise.

The second: for those who do good in this world there is good in this world, and this is in addition to the reward of the Hereafter.

Regarding what is meant by the good that they have in this world, there are four views. The first is well-being and health, said by al-Suddi.

The second is what Allah provides them of the good of this world, said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The third is what He gives them of obedience to Him in this world and His Paradise in the Hereafter, said by al-Hasan.

The fourth is victory and spoils of war, related by al-Naqqash.

And it may be a fifth: that the good in this world is praise, and in the Hereafter is recompense.

﴿And the earth of Allah is spacious﴾. Regarding this there are two statements:

The first: the earth of Paradise, about whose vastness He encouraged them, related by Ibn Isa.

The second: it is the land of migration, said by Ata'.

And it may be a third: that by the vastness of the earth is meant the vastness of provision, because He provides them from the earth, so its meaning would be: the provision of Allah is vast. This is more fitting, because He expressed its vastness in the manner of bestowing favor through it.

﴿Only those who are patient will be paid their reward without reckoning﴾. Regarding this there are four views:

(p-١١٩) The first: meaning without bestowing favor upon them and without following up, said by al-Suddi.

The second: their reward for their deeds is not counted only, but they receive increase beyond that, said by Ibn Jurayj.

The third: it is not given to them in a measured amount, but in abundance.

The fourth: abundant without restriction. The rajaz poet says:

O Hind, may He give you drink without reckoning, a drink from the King whose rababa is good.

And it is related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: Every reward is measured by volume and weighed by weight, except the reward of the patient, which is poured out by handfuls.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verses 13–16:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations:

The first: they lost themselves by causing them to be destroyed in the Fire, and they lost their families in that they will find no family in the Fire, though they had family in this world. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they lost themselves by what they deprived them of from Paradise, and their families from the Ḥūr al-ʿĪn (the wide-eyed maidens of Paradise) who were prepared [for them] in Paradise. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The third: they lost themselves and their families in that they themselves went to the Fire through disbelief, and their families went to Paradise through faith. This is a possibility.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verses 21–22:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam﴾ has two interpretations:

First: He expanded his breast to Islam until he became firm in it. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi.

Second: He expanded his breast with Islam, through joy in it and tranquility in it. According to this view, the expansion (sharh) cannot occur before Islam. According to the first view, the expansion can occur before Islam.

﴿So he is upon light from his Lord﴾ has two interpretations:

First: Upon guidance from his Lord. This was said by al-Suddi.

Second: It is the Book of Allah, by which he acts and to which he returns. This was said by Qatadah.

ʿAmr ibn Murrah narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Sidr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse, and they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is this expansion?' He said: '(It is) a light that is cast into the heart.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is there a sign of that?' He said: '(Yes).' They said: 'What is it?' He said: '(Turning in repentance) to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death.'"

Regarding who this verse was revealed about, there are three opinions:

First: It refers to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Second: It refers to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. This was related by al-Naqqash.

Third: It refers to ʿAmmar ibn Yasir. This was said by Muqatil.

﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾. It has been said that this refers to Abu Jahl and his followers among the disbelievers of Quraysh. In the speech there is an implied, omitted element, its sense being: "Is the one who is upon light from his Lord like the one whom Allah has sealed upon his heart? So woe to those whose hearts are hardened."

Third: It refers to ʿAmmar ibn Yasir. This was said by Muqatil.

﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾. It has been said that this refers to Abu Jahl and his followers among the disbelievers of Quraysh. In the speech there is an implied, omitted element, its sense being: "Is the one who is upon light from his Lord like the one whom Allah has sealed upon his heart? So woe to those whose hearts are hardened."

One of the two reasons is that it is the speech of Allah, and speech is called *hadith* (narration/discourse), just as the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was called *hadith*.

The second is that it is the *hadith* of revelation (*al-tanzil*), following the revealed Books that came before it, sent down to the prophets who preceded it.

The description of it as ﴿the best of discourse﴾ may bear two meanings:

One: for its eloquence and its inimitability (*i'jaz*).

Two: because it is the most perfect of the Books and the most firmly established in its rulings (*ihkam*).

As for ﴿a Book, its verses resembling one another﴾, there are two opinions:

One: that some of it resembles other parts of it in its verses and letters. This was said by Qatadah.

Two: that some of it resembles other parts of it in its light, its truthfulness and its justice. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

It may also bear a third meaning: that it resembles the Books of Allah revealed to His prophets in what it contains of commands, prohibitions, encouragement and warning, although it is more comprehensive and more inimitable.

Then He described it, saying: (p-123) ﴿oft-repeated﴾, and concerning this there are seven interpretations:

First: Allah has repeated in it the decrees. This was said by al-Hasan and Ikrimah.

Second: Allah has repeated in it the stories of the prophets. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Third: Allah has repeated in it the mention of Paradise and Hellfire. This was said by Sufyan.

Fourth: because the verse is repeated after the verse, and the surah after the surah. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Fifth: it is recited repeatedly and is not tiring to hear, because of the beauty of what is heard. This was said by Ibn Isa.

Sixth: its meaning is that some of it explains other parts of it. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Seventh: that *al-mathani* is a name for the final parts of the verses, so that *al-Qur'an* is the name for all of it, *al-surah* is the name for each section of it, *al-ayah* is the name for each division of the surah, and *al-mathani* is the name for the end of each verse of it. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it; then their skins and hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾. Concerning this there are three meanings:

One: that they shiver at its threat and soften at its promise. This was said by al-Suddi.

Two: that they shiver from fear and soften through hope. This was said by Ibn Isa.

Three: the skins shiver out of reverence for it, and soften when it is recited.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verses 27–31:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿A Qur'an in Arabic, without any crookedness﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

First: "without any ambiguity (labs)." This is said by Mujahid.

Second: "without disagreement (ikhtilaf)." This is said by al-Dahhak.

Third: "without any doubt (shakk)." This is said by al-Suddi.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man﴾ meaning the disbeliever.

﴿Having partners﴾ i.e., he worships various idols.

﴿Quarrelling (mutashakisun)﴾: regarding this there are four aspects:

First: "disputing with one another," said by Qatadah.

Second: "disagreeing," said by Ibn Ziyad.

Third: "difficult to please (mutaʿasirun)."

Fourth: "wronging one another (mutazalimun)," derived from their saying: shakasani maali, meaning "my property wronged me."

﴿And a man belonging wholly to one man﴾ meaning the believer, belonging wholly to one man, i.e., sincerely devoted to one man, meaning that by his faith he worships one God.

﴿Are the two equal in description?﴾ i.e., is the state of the one who worships Allah alone equal to the state of one who worships other gods besides Him? So He presented for them the example of two slaves, one of whom belongs to several partners who quarrel, unable to render each of them his full due in service, while the other belongs to a single master who is able to render him his full due in service.

﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ may bear two meanings:

First: for His argument through the example by which He refuted the polytheists.

Second: for His guidance, by which He aided the believers.

(p-125) ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ may bear two meanings:

First: they do not know the example that was presented.

Second: they do not know that Allah is the God who is worshipped.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die﴾. This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), informing him of his death and their death. It admits of five aspects:

First: that He mentions this as a warning about the Hereafter.

Second: that He mentions it as an incitement to action.

Third: that He mentions it as preparation for death.

Fourth: lest they dispute about his death, as the nations disputed about others' deaths; indeed, when ʿUmar denied his death, Abu Bakr argued with this verse, and he fell silent.

Fifth: to teach him that Allah, exalted is He, has equalized among His creation in this matter, despite their differing in other matters, so that consolation is abundant and grief is lessened.

The meaning of "innaka mayyit" is "you will die." It is said mayyit (with shaddah) for one who will die, and mayt (without shaddah) for one who has died.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾. Regarding this there are four aspects:

First: concerning blood, said by Ikrimah.

Second: concerning debts, said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

Third: concerning faith and disbelief, said by Ibn Zayd. The disputing of believers is a rebuke, and the disputing of disbelievers is regret.

Fourth: what Ibn ʿAbbas said: the truthful disputes with the liar, the oppressed with the oppressor, the guided with the misguided, and the weak with the arrogant.

Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi said: When this verse was revealed, the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) began saying, "What dispute is there between us?"

It admits of a fifth possibility: that their disputing is their referring to Allah, exalted is He, concerning what they contested over in this world of their rights specifically, apart from the rights of Allah, so that He may collect them from the good deeds of the one who owes them and place them into the good deeds of the one to whom they are owed.(p-126)

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 39, verses 32–35:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And he who brings the truth﴾ the verse.

Regarding "he who brings the truth" there are four opinions:

First: he is Jibril (Gabriel). This was said by al-Suddi.

Second: he is Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Qatadah and Mujahid.

Third: they are the believers, who will come with the truth on the Day of Resurrection. This was related by al-Naqqash.

Fourth: they are the prophets. This was said by al-Rabi', who used to recite: "And those who came with the truth and affirmed it."

Regarding "the truth" there are two opinions:

One: it is "there is no god but Allah." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Two: it is the Qur'an. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

It may also allow a third meaning: it is the Resurrection and the recompense.

Regarding "he who affirmed it" there are five opinions:

First: he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Second: the believers of this Ummah. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Third: the followers of all the prophets. This was said by al-Rabi'.

Fourth: he is Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. This was related by al-Tabari from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Naqqash mentioned it from Awn ibn Abd Allah.

Fifth: he is Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. This was related by Layth from Mujahid.

(p. 127) It may also allow a sixth meaning: they are the believers before the obligation of jihad (armed struggle in the way of Allah), who did so without desire for spoils and without fear of the sword.

﴿Those are the God-conscious.﴾ The plural was permitted in ﴿they are the God-conscious﴾ and ﴿and he who﴾ is singular in the form of its wording but plural in its meaning, according to the way of the category (jins, the genus), as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿That Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did﴾ — before faith and repentance. Another understanding: "the worst of what they did" refers to the minor sins, because they avoid the major sins.

﴿And reward them with their best reward for what they used to do.﴾ That is, He will reward them with the recompense of the best deeds, which is Paradise.

Allah says, "Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die in their sleep." On this there are three opinions.

The first: when Allah takes the souls at their death, He seizes their spirits from their bodies. As for the one that has not died, while it is in its sleep, He restrains it from acting while its spirit remains in its body.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verse 49–52:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿So when harm touches a man, he calls upon Us.﴾ It was said that it was revealed concerning Abu Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughirah.

﴿Then when We bestow upon him a favour from Us, he says, "I have only been given it because of knowledge."﴾ In this there are five aspects:

The first: "because of knowledge" of His being pleased with him (ʿalā ʿilm bi-riḍāhu ʿannī), related by Ibn ʿIsā.

The second: "by my knowledge" (bi-ʿilmī), related by Mujahid.

The third: "by a knowledge which Allah taught me" (bi-ʿilmin ʿallamanī Allāhu iyyāh), related by al-Hasan.

The fourth: "I knew that I would attain it" ('alimtu annī sawfa uṣību-hu), related by al-Naqqash.

The fifth: "upon a report that is with me" (ʿalā khabarin ʿindī), related by Qatadah.

﴿Nay, it is a trial﴾. In this there are two aspects:

One: the favour itself, because he is tested by it.

The second: the saying he holds to, because he will be punished for it.

﴿But most of them do not know.﴾ The trial is through blessings (al-balwā mina al-nuʿmā).

وَيَحْتَمِلُ ثانِيًا: أسْرَفُوا عَلى أنْفُسِهِمْ في ارْتِكابِ الذُّنُوبِ مَعَ ثُبُوتِ الإيمانِ والتِزامِهِ ﴿لا تَقْنَطُوا مِن رَحْمَةِ اللَّهِ﴾ أيْ لا تَيْأسُوا مِن رَحْمَتِهِ.

﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًا﴾ فِيهِ ثَلاثَةُ أوْجُهٍ:

أحَدُها: يَغْفِرُها بِالتَّوْبَةِ مِنها، قالَهُ الحَسَنُ.

الثّانِي: يَغْفِرُها بِالعَفْوِ عَنْها إلّا الشِّرْكَ.

الثّالِثُ: يَغْفِرُ الصَّغائِرَ بِاجْتِنابِ الكَبائِرِ.

﴿إنَّهُ هو الغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ قِيلَ نَزَلَتْ هَذِهِ الآيَةُ والَّتِي بَعْدَها في وحْشِيٍّ قاتِلِ حَمْزَةَ، قالَهُ الحَسَنُ والكَلْبِيُّ، وقالَ عَلِيٌّ عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ: ما في القُرْآنِ آيَةٌ أوْسَعَ مِنها.

أحَدُها: هو ما أمَرَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِهِ في الكِتابِ، قالَهُ السُّدِّيُّ.

الثّانِي: أنْ يَأْخُذُوا ما أمَرَ بِهِ ويَنْتَهُوا عَمّا نُهُوا عَنْهُ، قالَهُ الحَسَنُ.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verses 60–66:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And Allah will deliver those who feared Him to their place of salvation (bi-mafazatihim)﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

First: by their deliverance from the Fire.

Second: by what they gained (fazu) of obedience.

Third: by what they attained (zafaru) of the (spiritual) rank (al-idarah).

It may also bear a fourth meaning: by the arduous acts of obedience through which they traversed (salaku) a mafaza, a term taken from the mafazah of travel (the desert waste that one crosses), i.e., the difficult acts of worship.

(p-134) ﴿Evil will not touch them﴾ because of their freedom from it, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

First: they will not grieve, because they do not fear the severity of punishment.

Second: they will not grieve over what they missed of the reward of this world.

First: by their deliverance from the Fire.

Second: by what they gained (fazu) of obedience.

Third: by what they attained (zafaru) of the (spiritual) rank (al-idarah).

It may also bear a fourth meaning: by the arduous acts of obedience through which they traversed (salaku) a mafaza, a term taken from the mafazah of travel (the desert waste that one crosses), i.e., the difficult acts of worship.

(p-134) ﴿Evil will not touch them﴾ because of their freedom from it, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

First: they will not grieve, because they do not fear the severity of punishment.

Second: they will not grieve over what they missed of the reward of this world.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verse 67:

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ has three interpretations:

First: They did not magnify Him with His true magnificence when they worshipped idols besides Him. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Second: They did not magnify Him with His true magnificence when they called to the worship of other than Him. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Third: They did not describe Him with His true description. This is the view of Qutrub.

﴿The earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection﴾ has two interpretations:

First: His grasping means replacing it with another, due to His saying ﴿On the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 48], and this is a possibility.

Second: That is, it is within His power, like what a person grasps in his fist.

﴿And the heavens will be folded in His right hand﴾ has two interpretations:

First: With His power, because the right hand (yamin) signifies strength.

Second: In His dominion, as in His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ [An-Nisa: 36].

The folding of them in His right hand may also have two interpretations:

First: Their folding on the Day of Resurrection, due to His saying ﴿On the Day We will roll up the heaven﴾.

Second: That they are in His grasp while the worldly life still endures, like a thing folded up because of His dominance over it.

﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate with Him﴾. Safwan ibn Sulaym narrated that "a Jew came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Abu al-Qasim, God has revealed to you: ﴿The earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand﴾. Then where will the creation be?" He (ﷺ) said: "They will be in darkness near the Bridge until God delivers whom He wills."

He said: "By the One who revealed the Torah to Moses, no one on earth knows this except me and you."

قَوْلُهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ: ﴿And the Horn will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom Allah wills.﴾ فِيهِ وجْهانِ:

أحَدُهُما: أنَّ الصَّعْقَ الغَشْيُ، حَكاهُ ابْنُ عِيسى.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verse 71–72:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups (zumaran)﴾. Regarding it there are four interpretations:

The first: in companies (afwajan). This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: in nations (umaman). This is the view of al-Kalbi.

The third: in bands (jama'at). This is the view of al-Suddi.

Al-Akhfash said: "Bands separated from one another, one following another; its singular is zumrah."

Khufaf ibn Nadbah said:

"As if their going out at dawn, hurrying, from every hidden place, were in that they are zumar (bands)."

The fourth: pushed and driven with a sound like the sound of the mizmar (a wind instrument or pipe), and from their saying "mazamir Dawud" (the Psalms of Dawud).

[p. 138] His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Peace be upon you, you who were good﴾. There are three interpretations of it:

First: "You were good" means you were good through obedience to God. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: "You were good" means through righteous deeds. This was said by al-Naqqash.

Third: what Muqatil related, that at the gate of Paradise there is a tree from whose trunk two springs flow. The believers drink from one of them, and their insides are purified. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And their Lord will give them a pure drink﴾ [al-Insan: 21]. Then they bathe in the other, and their skins become fragrant. At that point its guardians say to them: ﴿Peace be upon you, you who were good, so enter it to abide therein.﴾ When they enter it, they say: ﴿Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us.﴾

As for the meaning of "you were good," there are three interpretations:

First: "You were blessed," said by al-Dahhak.

Second: "You were honoured," said by Tha'lab.

Third: "You were purified," said by al-Farra' and Ibn 'Isa.

﴿And they say: Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us.﴾ His promise, in this world, is that which the Qur'an came with. On this there are two views:

One: that it is His promise of Paradise in the Hereafter as a reward for faith.

The second: that it is His promise in this world of the victory of His religion over other religions, and in the Hereafter of recompense for faith.

﴿And He has made us inherit the earth, that we may dwell in Paradise wherever we wish﴾. Regarding this "earth" there are two views:

One: the earth of Paradise, said by Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu Salih, Qatadah, al-Suddi and most of the exegetes.

The second: the earth of this world.

If it is said that it is the earth of Paradise, then there are two explanations for calling it an inheritance:

One: because it came to them in the end as an inheritance does.

The second: because they inherited it from the people of the Fire. This earth is part of the recompense and reward, and Paradise within its earth is like the lands within the earth of this world, due to the resemblance between them, by analogy of the witnessed to the unseen.

﴿Dwelling in Paradise wherever we wish﴾ means their dwellings, in which they are rewarded, because they are turned away from desiring anything else.

[p. 139] Regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿wherever we wish﴾ there are two views:

One: wherever we wish, of rank and elevation.

The second: wherever we wish, of dwellings and pleasant places. If it is said that it is the earth of this world, then it belongs to the blessings and not to the recompense.

Its interpretation may bear two meanings:

One: He made us inherit the earth through our struggle, so that we dwell in Paradise wherever we wish through our reward.

The second: He made us inherit the earth through the obedience of its people to us, so that we dwell in Paradise wherever we wish through our obedience to Him, because they obeyed and so they were obeyed.

﴿How excellent is the reward of those who act﴾ may bear two meanings:

One: how excellent is the reward of those who act in this world, Paradise in the Hereafter.

The second: how excellent is the reward of one who obeys, that he be obeyed.

The second: that it is His promise in this world of the victory of His religion over other religions, and in the Hereafter of recompense for faith.

﴿And He has made us inherit the earth, that we may dwell in Paradise wherever we wish﴾. Regarding this "earth" there are two views:

One: the earth of Paradise, said by Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu Salih, Qatadah, al-Suddi and most of the exegetes.

The second: the earth of this world.

If it is said that it is the earth of Paradise, then there are two explanations for calling it an inheritance:

One: because it came to them in the end as an inheritance does.

The second: because they inherited it from the people of the Fire. This earth is part of the recompense and reward, and Paradise within its earth is like the lands within the earth of this world, due to the resemblance between them, by analogy of the witnessed to the unseen.

﴿Dwelling in Paradise wherever we wish﴾ means their dwellings, in which they are rewarded, because they are turned away from desiring anything else.

[p. 139] Regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿wherever we wish﴾ there are two views:

One: wherever we wish, of rank and elevation.

The second: wherever we wish, of dwellings and pleasant places. If it is said that it is the earth of this world, then it belongs to the blessings and not to the recompense.

Its interpretation may bear two meanings:

One: He made us inherit the earth through our struggle, so that we dwell in Paradise wherever we wish through our reward.

The second: He made us inherit the earth through the obedience of its people to us, so that we dwell in Paradise wherever we wish through our obedience to Him, because they obeyed and so they were obeyed.

﴿How excellent is the reward of those who act﴾ may bear two meanings:

One: how excellent is the reward of those who act in this world, Paradise in the Hereafter.

The second: how excellent is the reward of one who obeys, that he be obeyed.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 39, verse 75:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne﴾. Qatadah said: "Encircling (muhaddiqin)."

﴿glorifying [Allah] with praise of their Lord﴾. And their glorification is a pleasure (taladhdhudh), not a worship (ta'abbud).

Regarding His saying:

﴿with praise of their Lord﴾ there are two interpretations:

The first: with the knowledge (ma'rifah) of their Lord. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: they mention [Him] by the command of their Lord. This was said by Muqatil.

﴿And it will be judged between them with truth﴾, meaning with justice. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: "And it will be judged between them" means some of them between others.

The second: between the messengers and the nations. This was said by al-Kalbi.

﴿And it will be said, "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ Regarding who says this there are two views:

The first: that it is the saying of the angels. In this case, their praise of Allah is for His justice in His judgment.

The second: that it is the saying of the believers.

In this case, their praise may carry two meanings:

The first: for having saved them from what the people of the Fire have come to.

The second: for what they have come to of the bliss of Paradise. Thus His judgment in the Hereafter is concluded with praise, just as He began the creation of the heavens and the earth with praise in His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. Therefore it is incumbent to follow His example and take His guidance in beginning every matter with His praise and ending it with His praise. And success is from Allah.
